questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: Translation cost between disciplinary registers
questions.learningObjective: identify what is lost when an argument is moved from one field's register into another's
questions.stem: A chemist's finding is carried into a discussion about hospital staffing, and the version the group writes calls the finding robust, meaning that the measured effect was unlikely to be an artefact. What has happened in that move?

options.text: Robust named a statistical property in the source field and a general reliability in the new one, so the claim has become stronger than the finding behind it
Nothing has changed, since the group used the word its source used and has not misquoted anybody along the way
options.misconception: treats wording carried between fields as harmless when the sense of the word is what shifted

options.text: The claim has been weakened, because a technical word is harder for a mixed group to test than an ordinary one would be
options.misconception: reads a change of sense as a loss of force rather than as a widening of what is claimed

options.text: The group has done what interdisciplinary work requires, since every field borrows another field's wording to make progress
options.misconception: treats borrowing vocabulary as costless and so excuses a silent change in the claim's reach

questions.explanation: Words carry the standards of the field that made them, so a term that names one thing in a laboratory and something broader in a seminar changes its job while keeping its spelling. Here robust named a property of a measurement and becomes a general claim that the result is trustworthy, and the group has not noticed the upgrade. The second option checks only that the wording was reported faithfully, which says nothing about what the word was doing, the third mistakes a change of sense for a change of force, and the fourth turns borrowing into something free, which is exactly what this case shows it is not.
questions.hint: Ask what robust named in the field the finding came from, and what it now names in the seminar.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: Boundary conditions lost when a term travels
questions.learningObjective: spot the condition a source attached to its finding that the new use silently drops
questions.stem: One passage reports that a device's rotational stability was measured across a five-minute window in still air. A second group writes that the device is stable under ordinary handling. Which move has the second group made?

options.text: It has kept the finding and dropped both the window and the air conditions, so a result about still air is now a claim about handling
It has reported the measurement in plainer words, which makes the claim easier for the group to check against the passage
options.misconception: reads the change as a gain in plainness and ignores that the conditions of measurement are gone

options.text: It has carried the five-minute window over to handling, so the figure in the passage has been extended rather than discarded
options.misconception: thinks the original conditions were preserved when the word now refers to a different activity

options.text: It has confused a property of the device with a property of the air around it, so the object actually under study has changed
options.misconception: insists a confusion about what was measured when the finding was merely reported too broadly

questions.explanation: A measurement is a statement about something under particular conditions, and the conditions travel with the number whether or not the second reader carries them along. The passage fixed a window and an atmosphere, and the second group kept the conclusion and dropped both, so a carefully bounded result has become a general property of the device. The second option praises plainness and leaves the conditions untouched, the third claims the window was extended when it was in fact replaced by a new activity, and the fourth invents a confusion about the object studied that the two sentences do not contain.
questions.hint: List what the passage says about when and where the device was tested.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: Decisions a translator must make
questions.learningObjective: name the decisions forced on someone who moves an idea into a field with no equivalent for it
questions.stem: One field has no word for what another field calls a controlled comparison, and a seminar group must still write about the idea. What does the group have to settle first?

options.text: What the new name will and will not let a reader infer about rigour, since the two fields grade rigour differently
Which field's usage to follow, since agreeing on the word settles everything else the translation involves
options.misconception: believes a settled word settles the standards that the word was carrying

options.text: Whether the idea can be put into ordinary words at all, since some field-specific ideas resist general language
options.misconception: raises a possibility about expressibility and passes over what the chosen wording will claim

options.text: How many examples to attach to it, since readers mostly learn an unfamiliar idea from instances of it
options.misconception: treats illustration as the main decision and skips what the terminology will commit the group to

questions.explanation: Translating an idea you must also translate the standards the idea is judged by, because the receiving field will read the new word with its own thresholds in mind and will not know which parts of the original sense travelled with it. The first option is that problem. The second assumes a shared label produces shared standards, which is the assumption translators most often make and least often earn, the third treats the issue as one of whether ordinary words will do, and the fourth settles on presentation while the claim the term makes goes unexamined.
questions.hint: Ask what a reader in the receiving field will assume the new term commits the group to.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: Population assumption carried by an imported method
questions.learningObjective: identify the population a borrowed method already assumes before it is applied elsewhere
questions.stem: A group takes a rating scale from education research and applies it to a hospital's discharge planning. The scale was built for classes with a stable enrolment. What assumption travels with the instrument?

options.text: That the units being rated are already fixed and comparable, which a class register supplies and a discharge list does not
That the raters will be trained, since an untrained rater invalidates any rating instrument at all
options.misconception: names a real requirement for the instrument and leaves the population assumption untouched

options.text: That ratings will be repeated over time, since an instrument used once measures nothing stable
options.misconception: raises a design requirement and leaves the units being rated unspecified

options.text: That the instrument was validated before use, since an unvalidated instrument cannot support any claim
options.misconception: cites the instrument's record and passes over what the instrument assumes about its cases

questions.explanation: An instrument is built for a kind of case, and the kind of case is written into how it is applied and scored. A class has a roster fixed before the term begins, so its members can be compared with one another, while a discharge list is a stream of arrivals and departures in which the units differ in length of stay and in what happened next. The first option names that. The other three are all genuine requirements of rating work, and any of them could be raised about this application, but each is a separate matter, and putting any of them right would leave the mismatch in the unit of comparison exactly where it is.
questions.hint: Ask what the scale was designed to compare, and what a discharge list would have to match to be comparable.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: What a laboratory standard adds to a claim
questions.learningObjective: explain what changes about a claim once it is measured to a laboratory's standard
questions.stem: A laboratory reports a result that meets its own field's usual standard for reliability, and a seminar group repeats it as established. What has the group added to the claim?

options.text: A confidence the original claim did not carry, since a field's internal reliability standard is being read as a general warrant
Nothing further, since the result met the standard its own field sets for results of exactly that kind
options.misconception: assumes a field's standard travels with the result and settles every other field's question too

options.text: A weaker claim than before, because repeating a finding outside its field reduces how much the finding is worth
options.misconception: believes any cross-field move subtracts force and misses the inflation that occurs

options.text: A claim about causes, since a result held to a high standard of reliability is taken to show what produced the outcome
options.misconception: assumes that satisfying a reliability standard delivers a causal conclusion as well

questions.explanation: A standard of evidence is a promise about what has been ruled out, and a field states that promise in its own terms and for its own purposes. When a group outside the field picks it up, the detail of what was excluded usually does not travel with it, so what the reader receives is the confidence rather than the qualification. The first option is that. The second takes the standard at face value across fields, the third predicts a loss of force where the real effect is a gain in apparent force, and the fourth smuggles in a causal conclusion that a reliability standard never carries.
questions.hint: Ask what a field promises when it says a result is reliable, and whether that promise was made to this audience.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: Reporting a laboratory finding without overreach
questions.learningObjective: choose the passage that uses a laboratory result without claiming more than it carries
questions.stem: A laboratory reports that an instrument separated two groups of patients in a trial run at one clinic. Which of the four passages uses that finding without claiming more than it carries?

options.text: The instrument separated the two groups at one clinic, which is a reason to try it elsewhere and not yet a reason to expect it to work elsewhere
The instrument separated the two groups, and because the trial was run at one clinic the result cannot be extended to any other clinic at all
options.misconception: reads a limitation as a bar, so the passage discards a finding the trial does support

options.text: The instrument separated the two groups, which confirms what the clinic's own staff had believed for years about its intake process
options.misconception: credits the result to a prior belief and adds agreement that the trial does not supply

options.text: The instrument separated the two groups, and since the trial was carefully run the question of whether the instrument works can now be closed
options.misconception: treats one well-run trial as settling a question the trial was only able to narrow

questions.explanation: A single-site trial licenses one conclusion cleanly and one further step cautiously, and the first passage takes exactly those two. The second turns the limit on the evidence into a prohibition on using it, which throws away the result along with the qualification, and the third adds a retrospective agreement the trial never assessed. The fourth is the commonest overreach of all, since a well-run design tells you the design was sound and not that the question has been answered, and the instrument has been tried at one clinic on one occasion.
questions.hint: Ask which passage would still be defensible if another clinic ran the trial and found nothing.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: The qualitative claim a number does not license
questions.learningObjective: state the claim about meaning that a measured quantity cannot support
questions.stem: A survey of a museum records that visitors spent a median of four minutes at each display. A group concludes that the displays held their attention. What has the group added to the measurement?

options.text: A claim about interest, where four minutes records time present at the display and not attention given to it
A claim about popularity, which follows from a measurable share of visitors remaining near a display at all
options.misconception: infers a disposition toward the exhibit from the fact that visitors stayed in its area

options.text: A claim about the layout, since a short visit suggests the displays were hard to find on the floor
options.misconception: treats a duration as a diagnostic of the building and reads a cause into it

options.text: A claim about visit length, which is the one quantity the survey actually recorded in the field
options.misconception: reports the measured quantity as if it were an addition the group had made

questions.explanation: Time present and attention paid are two different quantities, and a survey instrument can record the first without any way of recording the second, since a visitor may stand at a display reading a label, waiting for others, or looking at the wrong thing. The first option names the addition. The second infers a disposition from mere presence, the third reads a spatial cause out of a duration that records no such thing, and the fourth mistakes the group's conclusion for something the survey supplied, which is the whole difficulty in this item.
questions.hint: Ask what the survey could observe about a visitor and what it could not.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: A rate used to support a claim about meaning
questions.learningObjective: identify the inference from a measured rate to a claim about what something signifies
questions.stem: A report notes that in one archive, 12 per cent of cataloguing entries carry two different dates for the same object. A group writes that cataloguers there did not know the date of what they were recording. What has the group done with the figure?

options.text: Read a property of entries as a state of mind among the people who wrote them, which the count does not record at all
Identified why the two dates differ, since a figure of that size can only arise from not knowing the date
options.misconception: reads a proportion as if it were a diagnosis and skips every other cause of the pattern

options.text: Measured how often cataloguing is uncertain, and the group's sentence reports the finding that was actually produced
options.misconception: accepts a claim about entries as a claim about the reliability of the work

options.text: Compared two groups of cataloguers, even though the report describes entries and never counts the people who wrote them
options.misconception: invents a comparison the passage does not contain and calls the count comparative

questions.explanation: A count of entries records a property of the entries, and the people who wrote them enter the count only as the source of the entries, so a rate of double-dated records supports a statement about records and not about anyone's state of mind. The first option names that step, and it is the step a group is most likely to take when a number feels like it explains something. The second promotes the figure to a diagnosis, the third mistakes a count of documents for a count of uncertainty, and the fourth claims a comparison between people that the passage never made.
questions.hint: Ask what the counted things are, and whether the claim is about them or about who made them.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: The generalisation a description does not license
questions.learningObjective: state the reach that a single described case does not support
questions.stem: A report describes how one archive handled conflicting dates, by recording both and flagging the conflict. A group writes that this is how archives deal with uncertainty. What is the limit on that claim?

options.text: It shows what one archive did, and nothing follows about what archives in general do when dates disagree
It is too thin a description to support any claim, since a single account is never evidence for a practice
options.misconception: denies that a case supports any general statement and so discards a legitimate move

options.text: It is well founded, since a detailed account of one case is stronger evidence than any survey could be
options.misconception: values detail over sampling and treats vividness as a warrant for generality

options.text: It should have been about dates rather than archives, since what the case actually recorded was a pair of dates
options.misconception: redirects the object of the claim and leaves the reach problem exactly where it was

questions.explanation: A described case establishes that something happened, and how much more it establishes depends on what else the group can show, which in this report is nothing about any other archive. The first option states the limit correctly and still leaves the case worth reporting. The second goes too far and says cases never support general claims, the third treats the vividness of a description as though it were a sampling argument, and the fourth reclassifies the subject of the claim without addressing the step from one archive to archives.
questions.hint: Ask what the report would have to add before the claim could reach beyond the one archive.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: Keeping a description at the level its warrant supports
questions.learningObjective: choose the revision that keeps a claim within what the described case supports
questions.stem: A draft describes one archive's handling of conflicting dates and concludes that recording both dates is the correct response to uncertainty. Which revision keeps the claim within what the description supports?

options.text: It shows that one archive recorded both dates and flagged the conflict, which is one workable response not yet compared with others
It adds a second archive's practice, so the conclusion now rests on two cases and no longer on one alone
options.misconception: thinks two cases are enough and never asks how the two were chosen

options.text: It removes the word uncertainty, on the grounds that the case concerned dates rather than anything undecided
options.misconception: tidies the wording and leaves the leap from one practice to the correct one

options.text: It argues that recording both dates is defensible in principle, which is the right level for a conclusion of this kind
options.misconception: moves the claim to a level it can reach without noting the move it made

questions.explanation: The draft's difficulty is that it turns an instance into a verdict, and the first revision puts the instance back where the evidence put it while saying that something can be learned from it, which is honest and still useful. The second adds a second case and mistakes a pair of cases for a pattern, since nothing says the two were chosen in any way that bears on the general question. The third edits a word and leaves the verdict standing, and the fourth does reach a defensible level, but only by silently exchanging what the case showed for what the writer thinks, which a reader cannot check.
questions.hint: Ask which revision reports the case and still leaves a claim a reader could argue with.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: Mechanism first, then evidence
questions.learningObjective: state what would have to be true for a mechanism to work, then say what would bear on it
questions.stem: A group claims that longer staff introductions reduce anxiety because newcomers learn who to ask before they need to. First say what would have to be true, then say what would bear on it. What should the first answer contain?

options.text: That newcomers do in fact go on to approach a person, since the mechanism needs a contact to be made at all
That anxiety can be measured on a scale, since a group that cannot measure the outcome cannot test anything
options.misconception: requires an instrument and leaves the step the mechanism depends on unstated

options.text: That the introductions are long in fact, since the mechanism turns on how much time the session takes
options.misconception: makes duration the hinge and drops the behaviour the mechanism actually requires

options.text: That anxiety drops within a few weeks, since an effect that is not immediate is not an effect at all
options.misconception: sets a timing requirement and passes over what has to happen in between

questions.explanation: A mechanism is a story about a sequence, and the first job is to name the step in the sequence that the outcome depends on, so that the group knows what it would have to see. Here the story needs newcomers to use the contact they were given, and if they never approach anyone the story has no way to work. The second answer demands a measuring instrument, which is a sensible requirement and not the step, the third makes the session's length do the explanatory work, and the fourth sets a deadline that the claim never mentioned.
questions.hint: Ask what the newcomers have to do for the proposed route from cause to effect to exist at all.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: What counts as support for a mechanism claim
questions.learningObjective: distinguish evidence that tests a proposed mechanism from evidence that repeats its outcome
questions.stem: A group proposes that longer staff introductions reduce anxiety by giving newcomers a named person to ask. Which of the four results would bear on the mechanism rather than restate the outcome?

options.text: Newcomer given a named contact asked that person a question in the first week, which is the step the story needs
Anxiety scores fell after the longer introductions began, which is the outcome the claim was about
options.misconception: takes the effect as evidence for the mechanism that was supposed to produce it

options.text: Longer introductions were sustained for a full term, which shows the change was not a one-off attempt
options.misconception: reports feasibility of the intervention and mistakes it for evidence about how it works

options.text: Anxiety was measured with an established scale, which improves how precisely the outcome was captured
options.misconception: credits the measuring instrument and treats precision about the outcome as support for the story

questions.explanation: Evidence for a mechanism has to touch the link rather than the ends of it, and the link here is whether newcomers actually approach the person they were given. The first result observes that step directly, and it is the only one of the four that could come out differently if the mechanism were false. The second confirms that the predicted outcome occurred, which is what the claim already asserted, the third establishes that the change could be sustained, which says nothing about how it works, and the fourth improves the measurement of the outcome while the link itself goes unexamined.
questions.hint: Ask which result would look different if the proposed link between cause and effect were not there.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: Opposite results explained by a design difference
questions.learningObjective: identify the design or setting difference that could explain two studies reaching opposite findings
questions.stem: One study found that written checklists reduced information missed at shift handover; a later study at a hospital where handovers had already been restructured found no effect. What best accounts for the disagreement?

options.text: The checklist was meant to change a handover practice the second hospital had already replaced, so there was little left for it to improve
The second study is mistaken, since an earlier study has established the effect and later work ought to agree with it
options.misconception: treats a prior finding as settled and discards the difference in settings entirely

options.text: The two studies measured different outcomes, which by itself explains why the results pointed in opposite directions
options.misconception: offers a possible cause without checking whether either study measured the same thing

options.text: Checklists work only in the first setting, so the disagreement shows the effect depends on which hospital is doing the handing over
options.misconception: accepts the conflict at face value and generalises from a difference in settings to a conditional law

questions.explanation: Before deciding that two studies disagree, a group has to ask whether they were studying the same situation, and here the second hospital had already changed the practice the checklist targets, which is exactly the circumstance in which an intervention can produce no measurable gain. The first option says that. The second rules the second study out on grounds of chronology, the third offers a cause that the account does not support, and the fourth converts a difference in circumstances into a general claim about where checklists work, which nothing in the two studies establishes.
questions.hint: Ask what the checklist was supposed to improve, and whether that thing was still missing where it was tested.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: Samples that differ behind the same phenomenon
questions.learningObjective: name the difference in who was studied that can make two studies of one phenomenon disagree
questions.stem: Two groups study whether new arrivals are better oriented after a written welcome pack. One surveys everyone who finished the induction; the other surveys only those who left during it. Which difference matters?

options.text: The second group studied only the people who left, so its findings describe a group defined by the outcome under investigation
The second group had fewer respondents, which is the reason its results point in the other direction
options.misconception: blames the size of a sample and leaves the composition of that sample unexamined

options.text: Both groups asked the same question, so the difference in findings must lie in how the question was worded
options.misconception: assumes two identical instruments cannot produce different results from different groups

options.text: The first group measured orientation well and the second measured it badly, so the findings differ for that reason alone
options.misconception: attributes the disagreement to measurement quality rather than to who was measured

questions.explanation: A sample defined by the outcome being investigated can report anything at all about that outcome, because whatever the intervention does, it will have kept some people and lost others, and the ones who left were selected by the very process the two groups are describing. The first option says this. The second treats numbers of respondents as the whole story, the third reasons from an identical instrument to an identical result, which is precisely what the two groups do not have, and the fourth blames measurement quality, which would have to be shown rather than assumed.
questions.hint: Ask who would be missing from a survey of only the people who left, and why they are missing.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: Comparing a finding with a differently sampled rate
questions.learningObjective: identify the mismatch that makes a comparison between two reported figures unsound
questions.stem: A study of volunteers at a city library reports that 40 per cent of signed-up users renewed a membership that year; the library's own register shows 22 per cent of all members renewed. What is the problem with comparing the two figures?

options.text: The study's denominator is people who had already signed up, while the register counts every member including those who never chose to join
The register's figure is the weaker one, since a study designed for the question is preferable to an administrative record
options.misconception: prefers one kind of source on general grounds and never checks what each one counted

options.text: The two figures cover different years, which is the only way two numbers for the same thing can differ at all
options.misconception: supplies a difference the account does not mention and settles the question with it

options.text: The study's figure is the one for people who care enough to volunteer, so it measures a group's attitude rather than its behaviour
options.misconception: recasts the discrepancy as a difference in attitude and leaves the two bases of counting

questions.explanation: Two rates are comparable only when they count over the same population, and here one counts over everyone on the register and the other over the subset that had already signed up for the study, so the difference between 40 and 22 may be nothing but the choice of denominator. The first option names that. The second ranks sources without checking what each counted, the third invents a difference in years and treats it as decisive, and the fourth turns a counting difference into a difference in attitudes, which is a further step the numbers cannot take.
questions.hint: Write down who is inside each figure's denominator before comparing the figures themselves.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: A case set against a rate
questions.learningObjective: identify the fault in using one case to overturn a population rate
questions.stem: A colleague states that a kind of delay runs at about 2 per cent, and answers a question about one delayed hospital transfer by repeating the figure. What has the response done?

options.text: It has answered a question about this transfer with a rate over all transfers, and a low rate cannot say why this one was delayed
It has answered the question fully, since a measured rate is the strongest kind of evidence available here
options.misconception: assumes a summary statistic is the right answer to any question about a single instance

options.text: It has misidentified the subject, since the figure was about delays and the example concerned a transfer
options.misconception: claims a mismatch of subject matter and leaves the mismatch of scale in place

options.text: It has confused two separate claims, since the rate and the example were both about the same procedure
options.misconception: suggests two claims are tangled when the problem is the level each one works at

questions.explanation: A rate answers a question about a population and a case answers a question about an instance, and a low rate tells a group that the phenomenon is uncommon without telling it anything about why this uncommon case happened. The first option says that, and the pair of things are compatible rather than in conflict. The second treats a summary as universally informative, the third claims a mismatch of subject where both passages are about the same procedure, and the fourth raises two claims when the real trouble is a single claim being asked to do two different jobs.
questions.hint: Ask what question the rate is the answer to, and whether it is the question that was asked.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: Naming the two fields a question joins
questions.learningObjective: name the two fields a cross-field question brings together, then say what each supplies
questions.stem: A group proposes asking whether a new appointment system changes how often patients miss follow-up visits. First name the two fields the question joins, then say what each brings. What should the first answer contain?

options.text: Operations and health services research, one bringing the system as it was actually used and the other a way of comparing outcomes
Health services research and economics, one bringing the funding of the clinic and the other the cost to it of missed visits
options.misconception: names a real pairing that would answer a different question about cost rather than about attendance

options.text: Medicine and sociology, one bringing the clinical condition and the other who among patients tends to attend
options.misconception: pairs fields whose shared material is patient attributes rather than the system change itself

options.text: Statistics and operations, one bringing the measurement of missed visits and the other the timetable the clinic runs
options.misconception: treats counting as one of the fields and leaves out the field that would explain attendance

questions.explanation: A question becomes interdisciplinary when the two fields it joins each have something the other lacks and need, and the pair has to be identified before anyone can say what the question is for. This one needs operations for how the booking system actually behaves in practice, and health services research for a way of comparing attendance outcomes, which is what the first answer says. The second pair would support a costing study, the third would support a study of who attends rather than whether the system changed attendance, and the fourth counts one field that is a method the others use.
questions.hint: Ask which field knows what the booking system actually does, and which knows how attendance is compared.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: A shared artefact used for different purposes
questions.learningObjective: describe what a shared artefact lets each field do with it
questions.stem: A hospital and a university department build one shared table of appointment events, which clinicians use to trace an individual patient's route and researchers use to count delays. First say what each side does with the table, then say what the sharing makes possible. What should the first answer contain?

options.text: That the clinicians trace a route and the researchers count delays, so each is doing its own work on the same rows
That both sides have adopted one definition of a delay, so their findings can be compared without explanation
options.misconception: assumes a shared artefact has produced a shared definition and so removes the need to translate

options.text: That neither side now needs to describe its data to the other, since the table already speaks for both of them
options.misconception: believes the artefact does the work of each field explaining its own evidence to the other

options.text: That the table has settled which findings are correct, since both sides now read from a single source
options.misconception: gives a shared record authority to decide between conclusions, which is an argument's work

questions.explanation: The first stage is what shows the second is possible, since the two sides are doing different things with the same rows and neither has had to give anything up, and a tolerance of that kind is exactly what lets joint work start where the two fields' definitions are still in dispute. The first answer states the two uses. The second supplies an agreement the table never secured, the third treats the artefact as a substitute for explanation rather than as a thing needing it, and the fourth makes a record into an authority, which only an argument can be.
questions.hint: Ask what each side would have had to abandon in order to read from the shared table this way.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: Why a shared definition settles less than it appears to
questions.learningObjective: explain why agreeing a definition does not by itself make a cross-field claim sound
questions.stem: Explain why two fields agreeing on a single definition does not by itself make a claim built across those fields sound.

answer.exemplar: A shared definition settles one question and leaves three untouched, and groups routinely mistake the first for the second. It settles what a term names, which is a real gain, because a disagreement that begins in vocabulary can waste an entire session. What it does not settle is what the term is being used to do. Two fields can name a case identically and still differ about what counts as evidence for it, how far a finding about it reaches, and what would have to be shown for the claim to fail, and a claim can be impeccably defined and still unsupported on every one of those counts. The second reason is that agreement on a definition is itself reached by someone, and the party that supplies the wording supplies the boundaries inside which the other party then has to describe its own work. A field that adopts a definition in order to proceed has quietly conceded the structure of the evidence as well. The practical consequence is that a group should fix definitions early to get past vocabulary and then treat the remaining standards as separate questions requiring separate agreement, because the point of interdisciplinary work is not to sound as though the fields already agree.

questions.explanation: A strong response says that a shared definition settles only what a term names and not what counts as evidence, how far a finding reaches, or what would refute the claim, and adds that the field supplying the wording also supplies the boundaries the other field must work within, so standards still have to be negotiated separately.
questions.hint: Ask what a definition settles, and then list what is still unsettled once the two fields share one.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: Why juxtaposition is not synthesis
questions.learningObjective: explain what a synthesis must do that placing two findings together does not
questions.stem: Explain why setting two fields' findings side by side in a written piece does not amount to synthesising them.

answer.exemplar: Juxtaposition is the arrangement of two things next to each other, and a reader is left to perform the joining, which means the joining may never happen. A synthesis makes the relation explicit and takes responsibility for it, so the test of a synthesis is whether it contains a claim that requires both findings and that neither of them states on its own, because a claim of that kind is the only thing that cannot be produced by summarising each source in turn. The second reason is practical. A paragraph that reports the economics finding and then the sociology finding has to make each report readable to readers who came for the other one, and the effort goes into explanation rather than into argument, so the piece ends up longer and thinner at the same time. The third is that juxtaposition conceals its own seams, because a reader who does not perform the join will believe the piece reported a consensus, and the writer who has not performed the join cannot know what that consensus would consist of. Joining is the work. Placing is the preparation for it.

questions.explanation: A strong response gives the test, that a synthesis contains a claim needing both findings and neither alone, and adds why the distinction matters: juxtaposition spends the writer's effort on making each source legible and hides the seams where the join should have been made.
questions.hint: Ask what a synthesis contains that two summaries, added together, would not.
